title: Setting Up the ADO.NET Project and Database
description: Create the Company database, Inventory table, ASP.NET Core project, and configure the connection string.

data.text: Before writing any data access code, you need a database to work with and an ASP.NET Core project configured to reach it. In this lesson, you will create the **Company** database with an **Inventory** table, set up an ASP.NET Core MVC project, and configure the connection string.
Create the Company Database

You will use SQL Server (or SQL Server Express LocalDB) for this module. Open **SQL Server Object Explorer** in Visual Studio or **SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)** and connect to your local SQL Server instance using `(localdb)\MSSQLLocalDB` as the server name.
Create the Database
Right-click the **Databases** node and select **Add New Database**. Name it `Company` and click OK.
Create the Inventory Table
Expand the `Company` database, right-click **Tables**, and choose **Add New Table**. In the Table Design window, enter the following SQL script to create the `Inventory` table:

data.title: SQL: Create Inventory Table
data.content: Run this script in the Table Design window or a new query window.
data.code:
CREATE TABLE [dbo].[Inventory] (
    [Id] INT NOT NULL IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    [Name] VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    [Price] MONEY NOT NULL,
    [Quantity] INT NOT NULL,
    [AddedOn] DATE NOT NULL DEFAULT GETDATE()
);

terms.definition: An auto-incrementing column. Starts at 1 and increments by 1 for each new row.
A constraint that uniquely identifies each row in a table.
Automatically sets the column to the current date if no value is provided.
A constraint that requires the column to have a value; it cannot be empty.

data.title: Table design tips
data.text: The Inventory table uses INT for Id, VARCHAR for Name, MONEY for Price, INT for Quantity, and DATE for AddedOn. These choices keep the example simple while demonstrating common SQL Server data types.
Create the ASP.NET Core Project
Create a new ASP.NET Core Web App (Model-View-Controller) project in Visual Studio or using the .NET CLI. Name it `ADO` or any name you prefer.

data.title: Create Project with .NET CLI
data.content: Run this command in a terminal to create the project.
data.code:
dotnet new mvc -n ADO
cd ADO

data.text: Install the SQL Server Data Provider
ADO.NET needs a data provider to communicate with SQL Server. Install the **Microsoft.Data.SqlClient** NuGet package, which is the modern, cross-platform provider for .NET Core and .NET 5+.

data.title: Install Microsoft.Data.SqlClient
data.content: Run this command in the project directory.

data.text: Add the Connection String

A **connection string** contains all the information the application needs to locate and authenticate with the database. In ASP.NET Core, connection strings are stored in **appsettings.json** under the `ConnectionStrings` section.

data.title: appsettings.json
data.content: Add this connection string to your appsettings.json file.

rows: Allows multiple queries on one connection

data.title: Production connection strings
data.text: Never hardcode credentials in appsettings.json for production. Use environment variables, Azure Key Vault, or user secrets for sensitive values. The Trusted_Connection approach is for local development only.
For production deployments, you would replace `Trusted_Connection=True` with explicit `User ID` and `Password` values, or use integrated security with a managed identity.
Read the Connection String in Code
ASP.NET Core's built-in dependency injection can provide an `IConfiguration` instance to your controllers. Use it to read the connection string from `appsettings.json`.

data.title: Reading Connection String in a Controller
data.content: Inject IConfiguration into the controller constructor.

data.text: The `_configuration["ConnectionStrings:DefaultConnection"]` syntax uses the colon (`:`) to navigate nested JSON keys. ASP.NET Core automatically binds the `appsettings.json` file to the `IConfiguration` service.
Create the Inventory Model
Create a model class that mirrors the `Inventory` table columns. This model will hold data read from the database and serve as the shape for create and update operations.

data.title: Models/Inventory.cs
data.content: A simple POCO matching the Inventory table schema.

data.title: Hands-On: Verify Your Setup
data.description: Confirm that your project can connect to the database before writing any data access code.
steps: Read the DefaultConnection string in the Index action.
Create a simple view that displays the connection string.
Run the app and verify the connection string appears without errors.
data.expectedOutcome: The app runs and displays the connection string, confirming the database path is correct.
